Background Myostatin negatively regulates muscle growth, and its inhibition by suitable proteins can increase muscle bulk and exercise performance. However, the reference values of serum myostatin in athletes performing strength training are still lacking. Methods A cross-sectional study recruiting28 male collegiate athletes performing strength training and 29 age-matched normal controls was conducted. The serum concentration of myostatin and insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1), grip strength, and body composition were the main outcome measures. We used regression models to analyze the correlation between serum markers and the physiological parameters. The athlete group had greater height, weight, BMI, fat mass percentage, fat-free mass, muscle mass, waist girth, grip strength, and estimated daily energy expenditure. Results The IGF-1 concentration was higher in the athlete group (324 ± 80 vs. 263 ± 134 ng/ml), but the myostatin levels did not differ (12.1 ± 3.7 vs. 12.4 ± 3.5 ng/ml). The reference value for IGF-1 among the healthy young males was 293 ± 114 ng/ml, correlated with age and height; the value for myostatin was 12.3 ± 3.6 ng/ml, correlated negatively with BMI, fat mass percentage, and waist girth after adjustment for age. Conclusion Myostatin level is negatively related to fat percentage, and serum IGF-1 is positively related to height. The reference values could provide a basis for future doping-related study. Keywords Biomarker Doping Exercise Reference value Fat-free mass http://dx.doi.org/10.13039/501100005762 National Taiwan University Hospital NTUH 99-M1401 Han Der-Sheng National Science Council (TW) 97-2314-B-002-014-MY3 Han Der-Sheng issue-copyright-statement © The Author(s) 2017 Background As a member of the transforming growth factor β superfamily, myostatin is a negative regulator of muscular growth and differentiation. Myostatin knock-out mice have three times more muscle mass than their wild-type counterparts [ 1 ]. Better functional performance is also observed without noticeable physiological compromise in these animals. On the other hand, nude mice over-expressing myostatin showed a cachectic phenotype with both skeletal muscle and adipose tissue atrophy [ 2 ]. Myostatin is translated into a 310-amino acid peptide, and cleaved as N terminal propeptide and C terminal active peptide. It is then circulated in the blood as an endocrine hormone [ 2 ]. The N-terminal propeptide is a potent inhibitor for myostatin. In a human study, a male baby born to a professional athlete mother in Germany was found to have a bulky muscle mass and loss-of-function myostatin mutation [ 3 ]. The serum myostatin peptide level was as low as undetectable in this male baby. It is reasonable to hypothesize that inhibiting myostatin can increase muscle mass and strength, and the sports performance of athletes. Another study revealing that the serum myostatin propeptide concentration in a bodybuilder was significantly higher than that in an untrained volunteer supports this hypothesis [ 4 ]. Strength training, a mode of exercise that can increase muscle mass, can modulate myostatin. Strength training inhibits intramuscular myostatin mRNA and protein expression in rats [ 5 ]. In a human study, similar findings were reported by Roth et al. that muscular myostatin mRNA level decreased 37% in healthy volunteers after a 9-week course of heavy unilateral knee extension strength training [ 6 ]. In addition, Walker et al. claimed that the serum myostatin peptide concentration, analyzed with Western blot, decreased 20% in a healthy male volunteer after a 10-week whole body strength training course [ 7 ]. Insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1), a downstream molecule of the growth hormone (GH), increases protein synthesis in skeletal muscle. IGF-1 transgenic mice have accelerated skeletal muscle regeneration. The hypertrophic effects of IGF-I infusion on muscle are well documented in animal models and muscle cell culture systems. [ 8 , 9 ] IGF-1 expression increased in a rat model of cardiomyocyte hypertrophy and in healthy volunteers doing strengthening exercises [ 10 ]. Using the C2C12 myotube model, a dose-dependent reduction in myostatin expression was observed on exposure to GH; this action was reversed by the GH antagonist pegvisomant [ 11 ]. We previously proposed that myostatin and IGF-1 could serve as a brake and accelerator mechanism for regulating muscle mass or function [ 12 ]. Based on this accelerator-brake model, we hypothesized that both IGF-1 and myostatin may correlate with lean or fat-free mass. Due to their ability to modulate muscle mass and function, myostatin and IGF-1 genes and their protein products might be a target for doping [ 13 ]. Myostatin-inhibiting antibody and muscle-specific expression of IGF-I were shown to increase the muscle mass and function of mdx mice, an animal model of Duchenne muscular dystrophy [ 14 , 15 ]. It is reasonable to expect improved muscle function after injection of exogenous IGF-1, myostatin propeptide, or myostatin neutralizing antibody, which will change their serum concentrations. However, we still do not have their reference value in the general population or in the athlete. Therefore, we conducted a cross-sectional study to investigate the reference values of serum myostatin and IGF-1 concentrations in male student athletes and untrained counterparts, and secondarily to determine whether relationships with body composition exist for each serum marker in the grouped cohort.

extracted_data.document_summary: The study aimed to establish serum reference values for myostatin and IGF-1 in healthy young males, including strength-training collegiate athletes and untrained controls, while investigating their correlations with body composition, age, and physical activity. Key findings indicated higher IGF-1 concentrations in athletes, with no significant difference in myostatin levels compared to controls. Myostatin levels were negatively correlated with age, BMI, fat mass percentage, and waist girth, whereas IGF-1 levels were positively correlated with height, fat-free mass, and estimated daily energy expenditure, and negatively with age. The document also provides context on myostatin's broader roles in muscle and lipid growth, cardiac function, and its levels in various clinical conditions and genetic polymorphisms, highlighting the relevance of these reference values for anti-doping applications.

treatment_details.dose_specificity: The study was an observational, cross-sectional comparison involving 28 male collegiate athletes (including weight-lifting and basketball teams) who reported engaging in strength training for at least one hour per day, five times per week, versus 29 age-matched untrained controls. No direct intervention or therapeutic dose was applied to investigate acute dose-response. The analysis established reference values and correlations with physiological parameters, adjusting for age and body composition. Myostatin levels in athletes did not significantly differ from controls, potentially due to sampling timing or a steady-state condition in athletes, precluding detailed dose-response comparisons within this study.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Unchanged between strength-training athletes (12.1 ± 3.7 ng/ml) and untrained controls (12.4 ± 3.5 ng/ml). Negatively correlated with age (β = -0.897 ± 0.295, p = 0.004), BMI (β = -0.268 ± 0.110, p = 0.018), fat mass percentage, and waist girth. Higher in patients with COPD (11.85 ± 4.01 ng/ml vs. 7.46 ± 2.21 ng/ml in healthy controls) and decompensated congestive heart failure (49 ng/ml vs. 32 ng/ml in normal), decreasing to normal after therapy. Lower in older men (7.0 ± 2.5 ng/ml) compared to healthy young men (8.0 ± 2.3 ng/ml). Elevated after a 6-month lifestyle intervention in obese children, associated with reduced body weight, fat mass, and BMI. Lower serum concentration related to metabolic syndrome, central obesity, low HDL-C, and high triglycerides in diabetic patients.
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Reference value for healthy young males: 12.3 ± 3.6 ng/ml (range 7 to 32 ng/ml in general population). Athlete group: 12.1 ± 3.7 ng/ml; Control group: 12.4 ± 3.5 ng/ml (no significant difference). In COPD: 11.85 ± 4.01 ng/ml (COPD) vs. 7.46 ± 2.21 ng/ml (control). In CHF: 49 ng/ml (decompensated) vs. 32 ng/ml (normal); 12.3 ng/ml (chronic HF). Age comparison: 8.0 ± 2.3 ng/ml (young) vs. 7.0 ± 2.5 ng/ml (older).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Negative regulator of muscle growth and differentiation; myokine affecting the growth of both muscle and lipid; mediates cardiac development; blocks adipogenesis.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Healthy young males (reference value determination), comparison between strength-training athletes and untrained controls, correlation analysis with body composition and age, and various clinical conditions including COPD, congestive heart failure, aging, obesity (lifestyle intervention), and diabetes with metabolic syndrome.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates muscle growth regulation; lower levels linked to higher BMI/fat percentage/waist girth; elevated in muscle wasting conditions (COPD, decompensated CHF); lower levels in older men (sarcopenia); elevation with lifestyle intervention suggests role in obesity management; lower levels indicate metabolic syndrome/dyslipidemia in diabetics. Provides a reference for doping-related studies.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Reduced after 4 weeks of swimming training (rats); no change after acute bout of exercise (rats). Rapid increase 30 min to 6 h post-single bout of isometric exercise in rats, returning to baseline by 24 h. Increased in cardiac muscle after infarction and exercise (rat); remained unchanged in canine models of dilated cardiomyopathy and chronic heart failure.
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Reduced after swimming training; rapid increase post-isometric exercise (specific fold change not provided but noted as significant); increased/unchanged as described for cardiac muscle.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Gene expression of myostatin, involved in muscle growth regulation and cardiac development.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Rats subjected to 4 weeks of swimming training, acute exercise, or isometric exercise. Cardiac muscle in response to infarction, exercise, and in canine models of dilated cardiomyopathy and chronic heart failure.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Reduction post-long-term exercise suggests a mechanism for exercise-induced muscle adaptation. Acute increase post-exercise suggests early muscle remodeling. Changes in cardiac expression imply roles in cardiac remodeling or stress response.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Subjects with polymorphism A55T reported to have higher body fat percentage, fat mass, and truncal adiposity.
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Higher body fat percentage, fat mass, and truncal adiposity.

analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Genetic study recruiting non-diabetic Asian Indians with myostatin polymorphism A55T.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Polymorphism A55T is associated with increased adiposity, indicating a genetic predisposition to higher body fat.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Higher in strength-training athletes (324 ± 80 ng/ml) compared to untrained controls (263 ± 134 ng/ml). Negatively correlated with age (β = -34.27 ± 8.89, p <0.001) and positively correlated with height (β = 360.5 ± 167.0, p = 0.035), fat-free mass, and estimated daily energy expenditure.
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Reference value for healthy young males: 293 ± 114 ng/ml (comparable to reported normal value of 297 ± 10 ng/ml). Athlete group: 324 ± 80 ng/ml; Control group: 263 ± 134 ng/ml.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Downstream molecule of growth hormone (GH); increases protein synthesis in skeletal muscle, leading to accelerated regeneration and hypertrophic effects; activates muscular satellite cells and counteracts muscle function decline.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Healthy young males (reference value determination), comparison between strength-training athletes and untrained controls, correlation analysis with age, height, fat-free mass, and estimated daily energy expenditure. Surrogate for GH/IGF-1 axis activation.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Higher levels in athletes suggest positive association with physical training; linked to growth, muscle parameters, and overall physical activity, implying significance in athletic performance and development. Establishes normal range and provides reference for anti-doping applications.
